title: dynamic-precision-orchestration-kv-shard-profiles
body:
Purpose
This note proposes a design for a runtime-level precision orchestration layer that coordinates kernel selection, KV-cache sharding, and scheduler decisions across mixed-precision model variants (INT8 / FP8 / GPTQ / AWQ). The goal is to make fine-grained, shard-aware precision decisions that improve throughput and cost while preserving end-to-end latency SLOs and KV consistency.

Summary of intent
- Introduce the concept of a 'KV shard profile': metadata describing the precision-compatibility, memory layout, and allowed kernel families for each KV shard.
- Define a small runtime state machine (precision orchestrator) that consumes workload signals (latency/queue depth/seq-distribution/telemetry) and decides on kernel families and per-shard precision mappings.
- Add a lightweight ABI/handshake between orchestrator, kernel loader, and kvcache to ensure consistent in-flight migration and atomicity of precision changes.
- Offer a staged rollout/testing plan, a compatibility matrix for model families, and a set of telemetry counters + sanity checks for safe operation.

Motivation / problem statement
Current mixed-precision execution paths pick kernels per op or per layer based on static heuristics at model load. This is suboptimal for two reasons: 1) it ignores runtime workload characteristics (e.g., short vs long sequences, chat vs single-turn), and 2) it treats KV cache as a monolithic object which prevents selective, low-risk migration of hot prefixes to lower precision kernels. We want to: reduce per-token cost by aggressive low-precision execution where safe, keep latency SLOs by routing critical prefixes to higher-precision kernels, and avoid full-model re-quantization or global fallbacks on capacity fluctuations.

Key concepts
- KV shard: contiguous subset of token-key/value arrays within the model's K/V cache. Shards are the unit of rehoming, migration, and precision assignment at runtime.
- KV shard profile: a small JSON-like metadata blob (kept in runtime state and persisted for durability) with fields: shard_id, shard_range, supported_precisions (list), preferred_kernel_families (map precision -> kernel-tags), memory_cost_estimate, hotness_score, last_updated_ts.
- Kernel family: set of kernels that are ABI-compatible and provide interchangeable execution for a given op shape (e.g., matmul-block-64x64-int8-avx2 / matmul-block-64x64-awq-cuda8). Kernel selection happens at per-op site but constrained by orchestrator decisions for active shards.
- Orchestration policy: declarative rules plus a lightweight heuristics engine decides mapping from shard -> precision under constraints (latency budget, memory headroom, error budget from quality monitoring).

Runtime state machine (high level)
States per shard: UNASSIGNED -> MONITORED -> PREFERRED_LOW_PREC -> MIGRATING -> STABLE_HIGH_PREC -> EVICTED (for TTL). A shard starts UNASSIGNED after model load. It transitions to MONITORED when first referenced. After enough telemetry the policy may mark it PREFERRED_LOW_PREC if stable. Migration is an atomic process that ensures in-flight requests touching the shard either use the old precision or the new precision consistently.

Example transitions (simplified)
- On first access: UNASSIGNED -> MONITORED (register access counter, latency samples, seq-length histogram).
- If long-running prefix with low variance and quality checks pass: MONITORED -> PREFERRED_LOW_PREC.
- If memory pressure + cost objective: PREFERRED_LOW_PREC -> MIGRATING (fork KV shard: allocate low-precision backing store, schedule async re-quantize of historical entries).
- When migration complete: MIGRATING -> STABLE_LOW_PREC (update shard profile).
- If sudden quality regression or eval webhook flags: revert to STABLE_HIGH_PREC.

Handshake / ABI for atomic migration
Requirements: in-flight safety, minimal stop-the-world pauses, deterministic fallback.
- Orchestrator issues a MIGRATE intent for shard S with spec {from_precision, to_precision, migration_id, timestamp, kernel_tag}.
- kvcache replies with a precondition: current_version, active_refs_count. If active_refs_count > 0, orchestrator can choose: wait for graceful drain or perform copy-on-write (COW) approach.
- Kernel-loader receives migration intent and preloads kernel families for to_precision (if not already resident). Kernel family provides a versioned ABI symbol table so calls can route to kernel_v1 or kernel_v2.
- During the MIGRATING window, the scheduler pins new requests touching shard S to use the new kernel only after the shard's migration_state == READY. Meanwhile, readers hitting older entries either read from the old backing store or use a small conversion shim that converts entries on-the-fly (expensive, used only for tail latency-edge cases).

Shard-aware scheduler signals and policy inputs
Inputs the orchestrator considers:
- seq_length_histogram (per route)
- per-shard hotness (accesses/sec, unique session counts)
- per-kernel latency P50/P95/P99 under current load (from runtime counters)
- memory headroom on device and host
- queued request depth and per-route latency SLOs
- quality telemetry: per-route evaluation loss/regression counters and human-reported flags
- cost budget / target (internal config)
Outputs the orchestrator emits:
- per-shard precision assignment (map shard_id -> precision)
- kernel warmup/loading directives
- migration plan (batched shard migrations with time windows)
- fallback policy (when kernel not resident or error rates spike)

Scheduling heuristics (examples)
- Short sequences (avg <= 32 tokens) get preference for lower-precision kernels if P95 latency preserved: these benefit from aggressive batching and quant kernels.
- Hot prefixes with high re-use but sensitive eval metrics (e.g., system prompts) are assigned higher-precision kernels to avoid quality regressions.
- During sudden queue depth spikes, orchestrator may promote some shards to higher-precision temporarily if low-precision kernels saturate GPU compute due to less optimized arithmetic; conversely, if memory limited, it may demote cold shards to low-precision to free memory.

Compatibility matrix and kernel tagging
Propose a simple tagging scheme for kernels: arch:precision:quant_backend:capabilities
Example tags: cuda:awq:matmul64:packed-weights, rocm:int8:gptq:kv-batched, cpu:fp8:x86-avx512:streaming-dequant
The orchestrator only selects kernel families whose tag intersects with the shard profile supported_precisions and the node's hardware capabilities. Add a small compatibility matrix file in repo maintained by infra engineers.

Telemetry and safety checks
Suggested counters (shard-scoped):
- shard.accesses_total (counter)
- shard.active_sessions (gauge)
- shard.migration_state (enum)
- shard.requant_ops_total (counter)
- shard.quality_regressions (counter) -> increments when eval trigger fails
- kernel.latency_ms{kernel_tag,op,precision,p50/p95/p99}
- orchestrator.decision_rate (decisions/sec)
Alerts and automated rollback triggers:
- sudden increase in shard.quality_regressions > threshold -> immediate revert of last N migrations
- kernel.latency_ms.p99 increase > X% -> mark kernel_tag degraded and refuse new migrations to that kernel

Testing and contract tests
- Unit tests for state machine transitions (including concurrent request scenarios). Use simulated active_refs_count to validate COW vs graceful drain paths.
- Integration tests that run small models with synthetic traffic shapes (short-chat, long-context, bursty) and verify cost/latency/quality tradeoffs.
- Fuzz tests: randomize migration timings and kernel failure injection to ensure rollback correctness.
- Golden-quality evaluation harness: run canonical prompts across precision variants to compute expected delta-perplexity or task-score; define accept thresholds per route.

Operational concerns and rollouts
Staged rollout plan:
1) Canary on internal fleets with forced policies: only migrate cold shards to INT8 for non-customer routes. Run for 2 weeks.
2) Expand to customer testbeds with monitoring dashboards and opt-out flag per-customer.
3) Open opt-in for dedicated customers to test in their private clusters (with audit logging).
Migration safety knobs:
- global_migration_rate_limit (shards/min)
- per-node_concurrent_migrations_limit
- dry_run_mode that simulates migration cost and outputs estimated latency/cost delta

Open questions / tradeoffs
- Per-shard granularity vs per-layer or per-attention-head: smaller shards improve selectivity but increase bookkeeping and metadata overhead. We recommend starting with coarse shards (e.g., 64-token ranges) and refine if telemetry shows benefits.
- On-device re-quantization vs host-side conversion: on-device is faster but requires more resident kernels and memory; host-side reduces GPU pressure but increases PCIe overhead. Policy should prefer on-device when node has spare memory headroom.
- Interaction with KV cache eviction: when eviction occurs, ensure shard metadata is updated and migrations are canceled with safe rollback.

Appendix: Example runtime migration sequence (narrative)
1) Request A touches prefix corresponding to shard S -> runtime marks S MONITORED and increments shard.accesses_total.
2) Over time, orchestrator observes S has low variance and high re-use; policy marks S as PREFERRED_LOW_PREC.
3) Orchestrator emits MIGRATE intent -> kvcache reserves COW backing store -> kernel-loader preloads AWQ kernel family for S.
4) As migration runs async, new requests are either pinned to the old version or, after a short grace period when migration reaches READY, pinned to the new low-precision kernels.
5) Telemetry continues to be evaluated; if quality regression observed, orchestrator issues REVERT intent which swaps back the mapping and triggers async cleanup.

Next steps / actions
- Engineering: prototype a small in-process orchestrator module that tracks shard profiles and can emit migration intents to existing kernel-loader/kvcache abstractions (owner: Ben Turner).
- SRE/Infra: add a minimal kernel-tag compatibility registry and extend node agent to report memory headroom per GPU (owner: Maya Chen).
- Applied ML: run golden-eval on representative models (Llama-family, Mistral variants) to create baseline quality deltas for INT8/AWQ/GPTQ/FP8 (owner: Diego Alvarez).

Notes and references
This doc is intentionally high-level; follow-up PRD will enumerate APIs, proto messages, and exact telemetry schemas. See linked artifacts for initial tickets and the compatibility registry draft.
